problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$

activity_context.topic_title: Double Integrals in Plane Polar Coordinates

examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral by Converting To Polar Coordinates
examples.problem: Integrate the function $f(x, y) = 15xy^2$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $x \geq 0,y \geq 0.$
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/051cfbbf3fd37f01ff7e4442fccdc5ec4ce506e3c452b68bfa2ed5ae6e5cf6b9.png)

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \:0\leq \theta \leq  \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({2}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =32({sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{3}⁡(0)) \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{2}^{4}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2}^{4}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =6(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$
